stances.claim: The prosecution can save time by focusing on three or four articles and waiving the rest -- one finding of guilt is enough to oust the respondent.

The Senate has wide latitude to control and shorten the proceeding without violating due process -- the Clinton trial lasted only five weeks with three witnesses and no re-authentication of documents.
Three propositions: (1) wide Senate latitude; (2) no binding judicial standard; (3) senators as people's alter egos have wide discretion in deciding the respondent's fitness.

notable_anecdotes: Clinton's five-week trial: House filed December 19, 1998; Senate verdict February 12, 1999 -- with only three witnesses (Lewinsky, Jordan, Blumenthal) whose oral depositions were reported in writing and video clips, not live testimony before the full Senate.
Starr's 36 boxes of evidence presented to the House were not re-authenticated in the Senate -- and no one complained of due-process violation.
Senators refused to be called 'jurors' -- addressed as plain senators; Chief Justice Rehnquist read their written questions aloud.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to Senate President Enrile's call to speed up the Corona impeachment trial, Panganiban offers practical suggestions: stipulate on authenticity of public records; the prosecution could waive most articles and focus on three or four (one finding of guilt is enough to oust); and the Senate itself can stop evidence presentation once it has enough to decide. He addresses the standard-of-proof question: impeachment is not a judicial case, so beyond-reasonable-doubt, preponderance, and substantial evidence do not bind the Senate -- even non-lawyers serve as senator-judges, and Enrile confirmed senators have their own standard. Using the Clinton impeachment (December 19, 1998 to February 12, 1999 -- five weeks) as the efficiency model: only three witnesses (Lewinsky, Jordan, Blumenthal) deposed off-floor in video clips; Starr's 36 evidence boxes not re-authenticated; senators wrote questions to 'managers' (not prosecutors) that Rehnquist read aloud; senators refused the title 'jurors.' The Senate voted to retain Clinton because the articles did not amount to treason/bribery/high crimes and Clinton's public approval remained robust. Three propositions: (1) the Senate has wide latitude to control and shorten the proceeding; (2) no judicial proof standard applies; (3) senators as the people's alter egos have wide discretion in deciding the respondent's fitness.
